column2: On the authority of Abū Hurayrah ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ṣakhr (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) say: “What I have forbidden you, avoid it; and what I have commanded you, do of it what you are able.
For what destroyed those before you was only their excessive questioning and their disagreeing with their prophets.” Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.
Both shaykhs [al-Bukhārī and Muslim] recorded this hadith, and with this wording it is in Muslim, in the Book of Virtues (1737).
The occasion of the hadith is explained in Muslim's Book of Ḥajj (1337), from Abū Hurayrah, who said: “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ addressed us and said: O people,
Allah has made Ḥajj obligatory on you, so perform Ḥajj. A man said: Every year, O Messenger of Allah?

He remained silent until the man had said it three times. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Had I said yes, it would have become obligatory, and you would not have been able to do it. Then he said: Leave me as long as I leave you,

for those before you were destroyed only by their excessive questioning and their disagreeing with their prophets. If I command you to do something, do of it what you are able; and if I forbid you something, leave it.”
His words, “What I have forbidden you, avoid it; and what I have commanded you, do of it what you are able”, make carrying out a command conditional on ability, but not [avoiding] a prohibition.
That is because a prohibition belongs to the category of refraining, which is within one's ability: a person is able not to do something. A command, however, is restricted by ability,

because it is a duty to perform an action, which may or may not be within one's ability; so the one commanded does what he is commanded according to his ability. For example, drinking wine is forbidden, and the one forbidden is able not to drink it; but prayer is commanded,

and he prays it according to his ability: standing, or if not, sitting, or if not, lying down. An illustration from physical matters is if a person were told: Do not enter through this door; he is able not to enter,
because it is refraining. But if he were told: Carry this rock, he may or may not be able to carry it, because it is an action.

Refraining from prohibited things remains general, and nothing is excepted from it except what necessity calls for, such as eating carrion to preserve one's life, or drinking a little wine to wash down something one is choking on.
The prohibition that must be avoided is one that signifies unlawfulness; what is prohibited by way of dislike may be done, though leaving it is better than doing it.

The legally responsible person does what he is commanded to the extent of his capacity—Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. If he cannot perform the act in its complete form, he performs it in a lesser form: if he cannot pray standing, he prays sitting;

and if he cannot perform the obligation completely, he performs what he is able of it. If he does not have enough water for wuḍūʾ, he makes wuḍūʾ with what he has and performs tayammum for the rest; and if he cannot give a full ṣāʿ for zakāt al-fiṭr but is able to give part of it, he gives that.

His words, “For what destroyed those before you was only their excessive questioning and their disagreeing with their prophets”: in his time, the questions forbidden in the hadith were those that would result in something being made unlawful for people because of the question,

or in something being made obligatory that involves great hardship and might not be possible, such as Ḥajj every year. After his time, what is forbidden is questioning that involves affectation, hair-splitting, and being occupied with it instead of what is more important.
The printed text reads قي زمنه, evidently for في زمنه (“in his time”).
Ibn Rajab said in Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam (1/248–249): “People have divided into several groups on this matter.

Among the followers of the people of hadith are those who closed the door of questions until their understanding and knowledge of the limits of what Allah revealed to His Messenger diminished, and each became a carrier of fiqh without being a faqīh. And among the jurists of the people of opinion are those who went to great lengths in generating questions before they occurred,

both those that usually occur and those that do not, and busied themselves with laboured answers to them and with much disputing and arguing over them, until hearts became divided as a result, and whims, rancour, enmity and hatred settled in them because of it.

This is often accompanied by the intention of getting the upper hand, seeking superiority, boasting and turning people's attention to oneself. This is what the godly scholars have censured, and the Sunnah has shown it to be repugnant and unlawful. As for the jurists of the people of hadith who act upon it,

most of their concern is to investigate the meanings of the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and what explains it of the authentic Sunnah and the words of the Companions and those who followed them in excellence, and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, knowing its sound from its weak,

then understanding it, comprehending it and grasping its meanings, and then knowing the words of the Companions and those who followed them in excellence in the various sciences, such as tafsīr, hadith, questions of the lawful and unlawful, the foundations of the Sunnah, zuhd, heart-softening matters and so on.

This is the way of Imam Aḥmad and those godly hadith scholars who agreed with him. Knowing this is more than enough to keep one from being occupied with innovated opinions that bring no benefit and never happen,

argument about which only breeds disputes and quarrelling and much idle talk. When Imam Aḥmad was asked about any of these hypothetical questions that do not happen, he would often say: Spare us these newly invented questions.”
He went on to say: “Whoever follows the way of seeking knowledge as we have described will generally be able to understand the answers to events as they occur,

because their roots are found in those principles mentioned. One must follow this path behind its imams, whose guidance and knowledge are agreed upon, such as al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Abū ʿUbayd and those who followed their way;
for whoever claims to follow this path other than by their way strays into wastelands and places of ruin, takes what may not be taken and leaves what must be acted upon.
The basis of the whole matter is to seek by it the Face of Allah and nearness to Him, by knowing what He revealed to His Messenger, following his path, acting on it and calling creation to it.

Whoever is like this, Allah grants him success, guides him aright, inspires him with right conduct and teaches him what he did not know, and he is among the scholars praised in the Book in the saying of the Exalted, ‘Only those of His servants who have knowledge truly fear Allah’ [Fāṭir 35:28], and among those firmly grounded in knowledge.”

He went on to say: “In sum, whoever carries out what the Prophet ﷺ commanded in this hadith, refrains from what he forbade, and is occupied with that rather than anything else, attains salvation in this world and the Hereafter.

Whoever contravenes that and busies himself with his own notions and what he deems good falls into what the Prophet ﷺ warned against: the state of the People of the Book, who were destroyed by their excessive questioning, their disagreeing with their prophets, and their failure to submit to and obey their messengers.”
It is obligatory to abandon everything that Allah and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ have made unlawful.
It is obligatory to do everything that Allah and His Messenger ﷺ have made obligatory.
The hadith warns against falling into what the People of the Book fell into, which was the cause of their destruction.
No more is obligatory on a person than he is able to do.
If someone is unable to do part of what is commanded, it is enough for him to do what he can of it.
Questions should be limited to what is needed, avoiding hair-splitting and affectation.
